PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 72 — Lesson 96: Asthma Management

FNP-level goal: Confirm or reconsider asthma, assess current control and future exacerbation risk, match anti-inflammatory and bronchodilator therapy to the patient’s phenotype and access, teach inhaler technique and action planning, and distinguish a manageable flare from respiratory distress requiring emergency care.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize asthma as variable respiratory symptoms with variable expiratory airflow limitation and understand why objective confirmation matters.
  • Separate symptom control, exacerbation risk, and baseline severity rather than relying on a single label.
  • Perform a focused differential for cough, wheeze, chest tightness, dyspnea, and nocturnal symptoms.
  • Use current guideline-based principles for ICS-containing therapy, inhaler technique, adherence, trigger reduction, and written action plans.
  • Identify severe exacerbation, anaphylaxis, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, and other red flags requiring urgent or emergency assessment.

Part 1 — Asthma Is Variable Airway Disease, Not Every Wheeze

Asthma commonly involves airway inflammation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, variable bronchoconstriction, mucus, and symptoms that fluctuate over time. Patients may describe episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, shortness of breath, nighttime awakening, exercise limitation, or seasonal symptoms. However, many people carrying an asthma label do not have objectively confirmed asthma, and many patients with asthma have normal examination findings between episodes.

When possible, confirm the pattern with objective evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation using current guideline-based testing. Spirometry with bronchodilator response, peak-flow variability, or other appropriate testing may help. Do not delay urgent treatment for a clinically significant exacerbation merely to complete confirmation. Conversely, do not keep escalating chronic inhalers indefinitely without reconsidering the diagnosis when the pattern, response, or objective data does not fit.

Part 2 — Control, Risk, and Severity Are Different Questions

Control asks how the patient has been doing recently: daytime symptoms, nighttime awakening, activity limitation, reliever use, and symptom burden. Future risk asks about recent exacerbations, systemic corticosteroid exposure, emergency visits, hospitalization, low lung function, high reliever use, smoking or vaping, poor adherence, incorrect technique, psychosocial stress, pregnancy, and comorbid disease. Baseline severity is inferred from the treatment needed to maintain control; it should not be assigned from one bad week.

A patient can report few daily symptoms but still be at high risk because of a recent severe exacerbation, no anti-inflammatory therapy, poor technique, low lung function, or an inability to obtain medication. The FNP must assess both symptom burden and the probability of a dangerous future flare.

Part 3 — Focused Differential for Cough and Wheeze

Consider upper-airway cough syndrome, sinus disease, GERD, ACE-inhibitor cough, inducible laryngeal obstruction, anxiety or dysfunctional breathing, heart failure, COPD, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, anemia, aspiration, foreign-body concern, malignancy, and cardiac ischemia when appropriate. In an older adult with new wheeze, do not reflexively call it asthma. In a patient with chest pain, hypoxemia, edema, unilateral leg swelling, fever, or systemic symptoms, broaden the differential immediately.

Ask about onset, triggers, work or home exposures, pets, mold, tobacco or vaping, occupation, exercise, infection, allergy, nasal symptoms, reflux, medications, pregnancy, sleep, mental health, prior intubation, ICU care, and action-plan use. Adult-onset or work-related asthma deserves objective assessment and early specialty consideration because continued exposure can worsen disease.

Part 4 — The Anti-Inflammatory Principle

Bronchoconstriction is only part of asthma. Anti-inflammatory therapy with inhaled corticosteroid-containing treatment is central to reducing exacerbation risk in contemporary asthma care. Reliever strategy and controller strategy should follow current guideline pathways, local formulary, age, phenotype, patient ability, and medication availability. Avoid simplifying asthma treatment into rescue bronchodilator use alone when anti-inflammatory treatment is indicated.

Before stepping up therapy, confirm the diagnosis, check inhaler technique in the patient’s hands, assess adherence and refill access, identify triggers, review smoking or vaping, and consider comorbidities. Escalating an inhaler without checking these factors can create cost and adverse effects without fixing the problem. Before stepping down, ensure sustained control, low recent risk, appropriate follow-up, and a written plan; do not withdraw anti-inflammatory care casually in a person at risk.

Part 5 — Inhaler Technique Is a Clinical Examination

Ask the patient to show every device, not just name it. Observe preparation, exhalation, seal, timing, actuation, inhalation speed, breath hold, dose counter use, spacer use when appropriate, cleaning, storage, and refill timing. Device mismatch, arthritis, vision limitation, language, cognitive impairment, cost, and embarrassment can cause apparent treatment failure. A spacer or a different device may be more important than a higher nominal dose.

Use teach-back for the written action plan: What medicine is taken daily or when symptomatic? What change signals worsening? When should the patient contact the clinic? When should they seek emergency help? Include school, work, travel, pharmacy, and caregiver realities. An action plan is only protective if the patient can use it at 2 a.m. during a flare.

Part 6 — Assess an Exacerbation Systematically

Compare today with baseline. Assess ability to speak, respiratory rate, heart rate, oxygenation when available, accessory-muscle use, mental status, fatigue, breath sounds, peak flow when appropriate and feasible, response to reliever medicine, fever, sputum, chest pain, hydration, and possible alternative diagnosis. A quiet or nearly silent chest in a distressed patient is not reassuring; it may reflect critically poor airflow.

Severe distress, cyanosis, altered mental status, exhaustion, inability to speak in phrases, poor response to initial rescue therapy, hypoxemia, hemodynamic instability, suspected anaphylaxis, or concern for PE, ACS, pneumonia, or heart failure requires emergency evaluation. The FNP must consider whether outpatient treatment is safe, not merely whether a nebulizer is available.

Part 7 — Triggers, Prevention, and Comorbidities

Address viral illness, allergens, occupational or environmental irritants, smoke and vaping, exercise, weather, reflux, rhinitis, sinus disease, obesity, sleep apnea, anxiety, pregnancy, and medication exposures such as nonselective beta-blockers or NSAID sensitivity when relevant. Prevention can include vaccination according to current recommendations, tobacco-treatment support, allergen or workplace-exposure assessment, and referral for difficult phenotype or repeated exacerbations.

Do not tell patients to avoid all activity. Appropriate activity and conditioning can improve function when asthma is controlled. Instead, make a personalized plan that includes pre-exercise symptoms, medication strategy under current guidance, warm-up, trigger awareness, and warning signs.

Part 8 — Referral and Longitudinal Follow-Up

Consider pulmonary, allergy, or asthma-specialty referral for diagnostic uncertainty, occupational asthma, frequent exacerbations, hospitalization, persistent symptoms despite verified technique and adherence, suspected severe phenotype, biologic-therapy consideration, recurrent systemic steroid need, or high-risk comorbidity. Referral is a partnership: send a clear question, record objective data and exacerbation history, and ensure the patient can access the appointment.

At follow-up, review symptoms, nighttime awakening, activity, reliever use, action-plan use, exacerbations, systemic steroid exposure, technique, access, adverse effects, lung function when appropriate, and comorbidities. A refill request is an opportunity to assess control and risk, not only a transactional task.

Part 9 — Clinical Case: The Label Needs Confirmation

A 28-year-old has been told they have asthma since childhood but now has daily throat tightness, normal spirometry between symptoms, poor response to bronchodilator, and high workplace stress. FNP reasoning: do not simply increase inhalers. Reassess history, objective data, technique, triggers, reflux and upper-airway symptoms, inducible laryngeal obstruction, anxiety, and occupational exposure; arrange appropriate testing or referral while maintaining safety precautions.

Part 10 — Clinical Case: The Patient Who Uses a Rescue Inhaler Every Day

A 42-year-old uses a rescue inhaler most days, has nighttime cough, and has avoided a controller because it is expensive. FNP reasoning: assess immediate stability, technique, access, current anti-inflammatory regimen, trigger exposure, and exacerbation history. A plan that assumes the patient can afford an ideal device is not a plan. Use current guidelines and formulary options to create an anti-inflammatory, teachable, affordable strategy with close follow-up.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: The Quiet Chest

A 19-year-old with asthma arrives after repeated rescue use, can speak only a few words at a time, looks exhausted, and has markedly diminished breath sounds. The FNP recognizes possible life-threatening airflow limitation. Emergency response and transfer override routine history taking or outpatient prescription adjustment.

FNP High-Yield Framework: AIRWAYS

  1. A — Assess urgency: speech, work of breathing, oxygenation, mentation, fatigue, response, and alternative emergencies.
  2. I — Identify the pattern: variable symptoms, objective airflow evidence, triggers, and time course.
  3. R — Review control and risk: recent symptoms, reliever use, nighttime symptoms, exacerbations, steroids, and admissions.
  4. W — Watch technique and access: observe devices, adherence, cost, language, and refill history.
  5. A — Apply anti-inflammatory care: use current ICS-containing strategy and a written action plan.
  6. Y — Yield to the differential: heart, clot, infection, upper airway, reflux, COPD, medication, and work exposure.
  7. S — Schedule follow-up and specialty care: objective testing, reassessment, referral, and closed-loop education.

Take-Home Summary

Asthma management requires both diagnostic discipline and practical teaching. Confirm or reconsider the diagnosis, assess present control and future risk, use anti-inflammatory treatment principles, inspect inhaler technique, and give an action plan the patient can use. Severe respiratory distress, exhaustion, altered mental status, hypoxemia, or a concerning alternative diagnosis is an emergency—not an outpatient step-up decision.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace current asthma guidelines, local acute-exacerbation protocols, medication labeling, spirometry standards, allergy or pulmonary consultation, or individualized emergency assessment. Severe breathing difficulty, cyanosis, confusion, exhaustion, or poor response to rescue treatment requires emergency care.
